cards.title: Eight Bits of Trust; eMudhra's CA keys cracked in milliseconds

depth.text: someone found eMudhra's **certificate keys** were tiny numbers, making them **crackable in milliseconds**

All eight intermediate private keys were **one-byte numbers**, so the researcher recovered them in **less than a second**. Chrome and Firefox blocked the intermediates, but many non-browser clients don't check revocation or CT by default; devices with **frozen firmware** may keep trusting them until July 2039.

cards.camps: Two camps: some suspect deliberate key use; others point to eMudhra's script-bug and human-error explanation.

Related: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50166579 “eMudhra intermediate CA compromise”

cards.title: One Hash Bloom Filters

depth.text: someone built a **one-hash filter** for Bluesky, but **removing mutexes** was what made deploys **much faster**

Jim Calabro's **gloom** splits a bit array into partitions and uses one hash to choose a position in each. Earlier, Bluesky's atomic version removed mutexes, cutting deploys from **90 minutes to about 15**. But the one-hash method itself brought **no noticeable speedup** at Bluesky, where contention—not hash count—was the bottleneck.

cards.camps: Two camps: one says hash mixing can generate extra indices without this partitioning; others say hash costs depend on filter size and warn partitioning can increase filter size or create hot blocks.

comments.text: You don't actually have to do this - you can stick with a power of 2 sized table and just gently mix the hash value to get each additional bit index. (source - I wrote MurmurHash/SMHasher and have used the above in my own bloom filters and cuckoo hash tables)

NB: You're trading non-negligible space efficiency here, which gets worse as you lower the false positive rate. Partitioning means uneven occupancy rates across partitions, and either you accept low occupancy (increased filter size overall) or you're pretty much guaranteed to have hot blocks (increased false positive rate for specific partitions).

While much cheaper than going to disk, computing k independent hashes per key is still a bit expensive for very high performance systems. Depends how big the bloom filter is. Most hashes are big and their bits are independent.

Gnutella and Gnutella2 used something like a single hash bloom filter to route p2p file queries across the mesh in a less wasteful manner. It was not perfect, but it worked enough to scale to very large user counts. https://rickcarlino.com/notes/p2p/how-gnutella-scaled-to-han...

I hadn’t seen that one hash paper before. This is a really cool optimization over Miztenmacher. Do you have benchmark numbers with different input sizes you can share? I’ll have to read the paper and code more, but it seems like this would be amenable to supporting filter merges as well (as long as the new size doesn’t exceed the filters’ capacity).

cards.title: The obscure trust looming over Anthropic's IPO

depth.text: an **obscure trust** can appoint **Anthropic’s board**, and commenters are asking what that means for an IPO

One commenter says the trust can **appoint Anthropic’s board**, which can appoint the CEO; another says the post leaves **few details** about when it might act. A commenter also quotes the article saying, “They own **no Anthropic equity** and don’t share in its profits.”

glossary.Interop: A project involving browser makers and others to get web features working across major browsers.
glossary.progressive enhancement: Building a website so its basic parts work first, then adding extras for browsers that can handle them.
glossary.container query: A CSS rule that can change an element’s style based on the size or state of its surrounding container.
glossary.reading-flow: A CSS setting that lets keyboard navigation follow the visual order of items instead of their order in the page’s markup.
glossary.CSS function: A reusable CSS instruction that takes values and produces a result, like a small recipe for styles.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.DOM: Document Object Model: the browser's list of the pieces that make up a webpage.
glossary.GHG: Greenhouse gas: a gas in the air that traps heat and warms the planet.
glossary.NDCs: Nationally determined contributions: governments' own climate pledges, including plans to reduce emissions.
glossary.overshoot: A period when warming goes beyond a temperature limit before being brought back down.
glossary.hysteresis: When a system's past affects how it behaves now, so reversing a change may not restore its old state.
glossary.certificate authority (CA): Certificate Authority: an organization whose certificates other software trusts to help check who a site or publisher is.
glossary.private key: A secret digital key that can be used to prove an identity or act as its owner.
glossary.intermediate certificate: A certificate that lets a trusted authority pass trust on to another certificate issuer.
glossary.TLS: Transport Layer Security: a way to scramble information as it travels between devices, so others can’t read it.
glossary.certificate revocation: Canceling a certificate's trust before it expires.
glossary.Certificate Transparency (CT): A public record of website certificates that browsers can check for suspicious ones.
glossary.CA bundle: A device's stored list of certificate authorities it trusts.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a scale people use to rate how serious a security flaw is.
glossary.proof of concept: A small test or demo that shows whether an idea can work.
glossary.session upload progress: A PHP feature that tracks how much of a file upload has finished.
glossary.multipart request: A web request that can carry files and other form fields together.
glossary.LFI: Local File Inclusion: a bug that tricks a website into loading a file from its own server.
glossary.ransomware negotiator: Someone hired to talk with hackers and try to settle what a company will pay after an attack.
glossary.phishing: A scam that tricks someone into entering login details on a fake site.
glossary.Tor: A network that sends your connection through volunteer-run servers to make it harder to link you to what you visit.
glossary.passive DNS: Passive Domain Name System: a history of which website names were matched to which internet addresses.
glossary.subdomain: The part added before a website's main name; here, it included the conversation title.
glossary.bug bounty: A program where a company invites people to find and report security problems.
glossary.zero-day: A security flaw attackers can use before its maker has a fix.
glossary.benzodiazepines: A group of medicines used for problems like anxiety or sleep; people can become dependent on them.
glossary.Ashton protocol: A gradual plan for reducing benzodiazepines instead of stopping them all at once.
glossary.taper: Lowering a medicine's dose little by little over time.
glossary.cold turkey: Stopping a drug all at once instead of reducing it gradually.
glossary.PRN: Pro re nata: a medical note meaning to take a medicine only when needed.
glossary.OSINT: Open-Source Intelligence: using information anyone can access to learn about a person or subject.
glossary.DarkINT: A name for investigating information found on the dark web.
glossary.NSFW: Not Safe For Work: a warning that something may be awkward or unsuitable to view around coworkers.
glossary.PGP key: Pretty Good Privacy key: a digital key used to protect messages or check who sent them.
glossary.crypto address: A string of characters used to send or receive cryptocurrency.
glossary.node: A point in a graph that represents something connected to other points.
glossary.use-after-free (UAF): A bug where a program keeps using a piece of memory after it has been freed.
glossary.prefork: A server setup that starts worker processes ahead of time and reuses them for requests.
glossary.ASAN: AddressSanitizer: a tool that checks programs for certain memory errors.
glossary.convertible notes: Loans that can later turn into company shares.
glossary.accounting charge: An amount recorded as a loss in company accounts; it does not always mean cash was paid out.
glossary.H1: Short for the first half of a year.
glossary.Bloom filter: A compact way to check whether something is on a list; it can sometimes say yes when it isn't.
glossary.hash: A label calculated from data that Git uses to locate stored content.
glossary.partition: One section of a larger thing that has been split into parts.
glossary.mutex: A lock that makes sure only one piece of work at a time uses protected code.
glossary.contention: When tasks compete to use the same thing, slowing one another down.
glossary.false positive rate: How often a filter says an item is present when it actually isn't.
glossary.VPS: Virtual Private Server: a computer you rent and leave online to run your own software.
glossary.LAMP: Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP: a common set of tools used together to run a website.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.MOOCs: Massive Open Online Courses: online classes designed for lots of people to take.
glossary.Lindy Effect: The idea that, for things that can keep going, having lasted a long time may be a sign they’ll last longer.
glossary.endowments: Money or property given to an institution to help support its work over time.
glossary.AI agent: An autonomous computer program that can carry out tasks.
glossary.tool loop: A repeating process where an AI uses a tool, checks what happened, and decides what to do next.
glossary.acoustic surveys: A way to estimate what lives underwater by using sound.
glossary.genetic diversity: The range of inherited traits found among members of a group.
glossary.parsimonious explanation: An explanation that accounts for what happened with the fewest extra assumptions.
glossary.dispersants: Chemicals used to break up oil slicks.
glossary.daemon: A program that runs in the background and handles a task without being started each time.
glossary.PDF: Portable Document Format: a file type that keeps a document’s pages laid out the same when opened or printed.
glossary.JVM: Java Virtual Machine: software that runs programs built for Java's runtime.
glossary.product-market fit: When enough customers want a product for it to work as a business.
glossary.citogenesis: A claim gets copied between sources until later writers treat those sources as proof.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall: a website’s guard that checks incoming requests and can block suspicious ones.
glossary.trait solver: The part of Rust that checks whether code has the behavior it needs available.
glossary.Polonius: A newer way for Rust to check whether code uses shared data safely.
glossary.soundness bug: A flaw that lets proof-checking software accept a false result.
glossary.LLVM: A set of tools that helps turn source code into instructions a computer can run.
glossary.artifacts: Files a build creates and saves for later use.
glossary.cam lock: A fitting you turn to pull two furniture panels tight together.
glossary.cam screw: A screw whose head fits into a cam lock, so turning the lock pulls panels together.
glossary.dowel: A small wooden peg used to line up furniture pieces.
glossary.racking: When a bookcase shifts out of its square shape instead of staying straight.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.equity: Ownership in a company, rather than lending it money.
glossary.trust: A legal arrangement where people are put in charge of managing something under agreed rules.
